deep_dive_html:
The Perils of Unconditional Personal Guarantees

For franchisees, the personal guarantee is often the most dangerous provision in a commercial lease. Landlords frequently insist on 'unconditional and irrevocable' guarantees that do not merely cover unpaid rent, but extend to all damages, legal fees, and even future defaults. This structure effectively bypasses the corporate veil of your LLC, placing your personal residence, savings, and future earnings at direct risk of seizure should the franchise underperform.

The most insidious version of this clause is the 'Continuing Guarantee.' In this scenario, your personal liability does not terminate when the lease ends; instead, it persists as long as any obligation under the lease remains unsatisfied. If a landlord claims damages for a breach occurring at the end of the term, you could find yourself litigating years after you have shuttered the location.

Negotiating Market-Standard Protections

To protect your personal estate, you must move away from absolute guarantees and toward 'Good Guy' clauses or 'Burn-off' provisions. A 'Good Guy' clause limits your personal liability to the period during which you occupy the premises and maintain the space in good condition. Once you provide proper notice of surrender and vacate the property, your personal obligation terminates, leaving only the corporate entity liable for any remaining lease obligations.

Furthermore, sophisticated franchisees should negotiate 'Burn-off' provisions. These clauses stipulate that the personal guarantee expires entirely after a predetermined period, such as the first 36 or 48 months of the lease, provided the tenant has remained in good standing. This allows the business to build equity and stability before the landlord can access your personal assets.

  • Seek 'Good Guy' language to cap liability upon surrender.
  • Negotiate a 'Burn-off' period to eliminate the guarantee after several years.
  • Ensure the guarantee is limited to 'accrued' rent rather than 'future' rent obligations.
  • Explicitly exclude consequential damages and attorney fees from the personal scope.
